arXiv:2610.23503v1 [cs.AR] 16 Oct 2026 HBFSim: A Simulator for Exploring HBF in Memory Hierarchies for LLMs Jinheng Li Guosheng Wang Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates jinheng.li@mbzuai.ac.ae Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates guosheng.wang@mbzuai.ac.ae Hongchao Du Shangyu Wu Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates hongchao.du@mbzuai.ac.ae Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates shangyu.wu@mbzuai.ac.ae Qiao Li Chun Jason Xue Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates qiao.li@mbzuai.ac.ae Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates jason.xue@mbzuai.ac.ae ABSTRACT KEYWORDS High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advan- tage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for het- erogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application- level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a cal- ibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0–19.0× faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences’ KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 11 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3848591.3856870 1 INTRODUCTION Memory capacity has emerged as a primary bottleneck in serv- ing large language models (LLMs). Model weights occupy tens to hundreds of gigabytes, while key–value (KV) state grows linearly with context length and request concurrency, quickly exceeding accelerator memory capacity. For example, an 8B model serving eight concurrent 128K-context sessions can exhaust the HBM of a modern GPU (e.g., the 131 GiB of HBM3e on an NVIDIA H200), while long-context serving for 70B-class models may exceed the memory capacity of an entire eight-GPU node [5, 11, 17, 22]. High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising ap- proach for extending accelerator-local memory capacity. SanDisk’s disclosed HBF design targets a 16-die, 512 GB flash stack that deliv- ers up to 1.6 TB/s [24, 25], enabling multi-terabyte accelerator-local memory systems without host-memory accesses. The same disclo- sure targets 8–16× HBM capacity at similar cost and bandwidth, making capacity per dollar, rather than higher speed, the main motivation for HBF [24]. Unlike conventional DRAM expansion, HBF brings asymmet- ric read and write performance, page programming, flash transla- tion layer (FTL) management, write amplification, and finite pro- gram/erase endurance into the accelerator memory hierarchy. Its effect on LLM serving is difficult to predict because no public HBF hardware is available for validation [28]. Nevertheless, system archi- tects must decide on memory organization, placement policies, and provisioning before production devices become available. For ex- ample, moving read-only weights to HBF mainly exercises its read RACS ’26, November 17–20, 2026, Fukuoka, Japan Weights H200 131 GiB 200 KV cache, 1M-token context five simple rules: HBF pays off only under capacity pressure; HBM should hold the running KV and HBF the weights, with KV written to flash only when it must leave HBM; generic cache replacement loses to this placement unless a step fits in HBM with room to spare; the FTL should preserve the flash array’s parallelism; and endurance, set by how much KV reaches flash, is a first-order constraint. 8×H200 1051 GiB 8 HBM4 stacks 384 GiB Kimi K3 Qwen3.8-2.4T DeepSeek-V4-Pro 377 Llama 3.1 405B 625 DeepSeek-V3 219 +188 Qwen3-235B +320 Llama 3.1 70B 66 7+128 135 Llama 3.1 8B 0 Li et al. 2608+27 = 2635 2235+92 = 2327 1490+10 = 1500 881 +504 +69 694 407 386 400 600 800 1000 1200 Weights + KV cache (GiB) Figure 1: Weights (one byte per parameter) and BF16 KV cache of a 1M-token context against the HBM of one H200, eight HBM4 stacks, and an eight-H200 node. path and frees HBM for the growing KV cache, whereas placing mu- table KV state in HBF creates program traffic and consumes write endurance. Therefore, it is necessary to study the performance of HBM+HBF memory hierarchies under realistic LLM serving work- loads before committing to a design. Because such hardware is unavailable, a simulator is required to evaluate these trade-offs. Existing simulators each cover one level of this hierarchy: DRAM simulators [14, 16] stop at the memory controller, SSD simula- tors [13, 29] put flash behind a storage interface, and LLM serving simulators [4, 10, 36] represent memory by capacity and bandwidth. None connects the placement of LLM data to both completion time and physical flash traffic. HBFSim addresses this limitation. It models HBM, HBF with a host-managed FTL, and conventional capacity tiers in one event system, coupled in a closed loop with a serving frontend whose scheduler and GPU compute are calibrated against measurements, and it accepts address-level traces as well as production request traces. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. We find that HBF serves the data that does not fit in HBM 11.0–19.0× faster than host DRAM; that HBM should hold the running sequences’ KV, because caching HBF with LRU or FIFO rereads nearly the whole working set once it exceeds HBM, and that KV should be written to HBF only when it must leave HBM; and that the FTL costs little on the read path as long as its layout keeps reads parallel, while HBF’s lifetime depends on the amount of KV that reaches flash. These findings connect HBF’s potential cost-per-bit advantage to measurable latency and wear rather than to a single capacity or bandwidth number. This paper makes the following contributions: • Workloads at two granularities. HBFSim takes fine- grained address-level traces, with one record per memory access, and coarse-grained request traces, which its frontend expands into the series of weight and KV accesses that each request causes. • A coupled and fast memory-system model. HBM, HBF with a host-managed FTL, and external tiers (host DRAM, CXL SSDs, and NVMe SSDs) share one timeline and interact as in a real system, for example through the FTL’s tables in HBM. • Preliminary takeaways for HBF. Decoding Llama-3.1- 70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads yields 2 BACKGROUND 2.1 Memory Demand of LLM Serving A serving system’s memory holds the model weights, which every request reuses; the KV cache, the per-layer keys and values of every processed token, which decoding reads instead of recomputing; and activations, which are small by comparison. For Llama-3.1-70B a BF16 KV cache takes 320 KiB per token [5], 320 GiB for 1M tokens. Serving systems allocate KV in fixed-size blocks [11] and retain the blocks of finished requests so that later requests with the same prefix skip its prefill [22, 37], so the KV footprint grows beyond the active requests. Figure 1 shows the weights and the KV cache of 1M tokens, in one request or retained across many: for small models the KV cache dominates, every model from 70B up exceeds eight HBM4 stacks, and the newest open models, with 1.6T to 2.8T parameters, exceed even an eight-H200 node with their weights alone, while hybrid or compressed attention keeps their KV small. The two phases of a request access this data differently. Prefill processes the prompt, produces its KV, and is usually compute- bound; chunked prefill lets it share a batch with decoding work [2]. Each decoding step generates one token per request: it reuses the weights across the batch, reads every running request’s KV, and appends one token’s KV per layer, so it is usually bound by memory bandwidth, and its traffic grows with model size, batch, and context. When weights and KV exceed HBM, systems offload to host DRAM or SSDs [15, 22, 26], at access costs set by the slower tier and its interconnect. 2.2 High Bandwidth Flash HBF stacks NAND flash dies on a logic base die and connects them to the accelerator through an HBM-like interface in the same pack- age [24, 25]. The OCP HBF specification [19] defines stacks with up to 16 channels and three speed grades. For example, at speed grade 2 each channel carries 96 GB/s of payload, or about 1.5 TB/s per stack, and SanDisk targets 512 GB per stack. An HBF stack therefore offers 8-16 times the capacity of an HBM stack at a similar interface bandwidth. However, HBF still behaves like NAND. A page read takes mi- croseconds, compared to tens of nanoseconds of DRAM, so HBF reaches its bandwidth only with many reads in flight. Data is pro- grammed, not overwritten: a page program takes tens of microsec- onds and occupies its bank, and a block must be erased before its pages are programmed again. The specification assigns address mapping, garbage collection (GC), and wear leveling to host soft- ware; the device itself performs neither GC nor copyback [19]. Each block tolerates a limited number of program/erase (P/E) cycles, and no P/E rating for HBF has been published. Host decisions thus shape both performance and lifetime: what the host places in HBF HBFSim RACS ’26, November 17–20, 2026, Fukuoka, Japan Serving frontend Request traces arrivals, lengths, prefix hashes batch time Scheduler batching, paged KV, prefix cache Compiler layer DAG: reads, writes, prefetch GPU timing calibrated kernels, memory overlap Peer mode each object in either memory; HBM first to the weights or the running KV objects → device addresses Tiered mode HBM caches HBF in 4 MiB lines: LRU, FIFO, decayed LFU; write-back transactions with dependencies Device engine one timeline, per-resource calendars memory feedback object accesses Memory policies Host FTL: mapping, GC, wear leveling tables, GC copies HBM channels, arbitration HBF device channels, planes, page buffers; read, program, erase timing; device DRAM buffer and cache Other tiers host DRAM, CXL SSD, NVMe SSD: link, controller, media results: time per output token, bytes per object class and device, programs and erases per block Figure 2: HBFSim structure: three layers. Feedback from the device engine closes the loop to the scheduler, and the host FTL keeps its tables and GC copies in HBM. determines the traffic HBF sees, and the host’s flash translation layer (FTL) determines how many erases each write costs. 2.3 Questions for HBM+HBF Systems Before HBF hardware is available, system designers need to answer five questions. Is HBF a better capacity tier than host DRAM or SSDs? How much HBM should accompany it? Which data should stay in HBM, and should HBM act as a cache for HBF or as sepa- rately addressed memory? How should the FTL handle KV writes? How long will HBF last under serving traffic? The answers depend on each other through the serving loop: slower memory stretches decoding steps, which changes how requests are batched and there- fore the memory traffic itself. Answering them requires running a real serving scheduler against memory models that include flash management, with the two coupled in a closed loop. 3 HBFSIM DESIGN HBFSim is a closed-loop simulator of LLM serving on accelerator memory built from HBM, HBF, and other capacity tiers. Figure 2 shows its three layers. A serving frontend turns request traces into batches and the requests in each batch into memory accesses. A policy layer decides in which memory each object is stored and how data moves between tiers. A device engine executes the memory transactions on models of HBM, HBF, or external capacity tiers, and feeds the outcome of that work back to the frontend, which schedules the next batch based on the feedback. Slower memory therefore reshapes batching as it would on a real system: longer iterations let more requests queue before the next one starts, and when KV no longer fits, the scheduler moves some KV to a slower tier or preempts requests, which shrinks the batch. Three challenges shape this design. Workloads and device accesses differ in granularity and semantics. A serving system works with requests, weights, and KV blocks; HBM serves data bursts of tens of bytes; and HBF is accessed like memory but programs flash pages (e.g., 4 KiB) in order, erases whole flash blocks, and leaves its FTL to the host. Address-level traces preserve individual accesses but can only cover short runs, whereas production request traces cover long periods of serving but record no memory accesses. The levels of the memory hierarchy are coupled. Existing simulators model one level in isolation, but in an HBM+HBF sys- tem the two levels jointly determine performance. What HBF must serve depends on what HBM can hold, and the traffic HBF gener- ates in turn consumes HBM capacity and bandwidth. Placement decisions therefore shift load between the tiers rather than simply adding a slower level beneath HBM, so neither tier can be simulated independently. The number of events is huge. One decoding step of a 70B model reads tens of millions of flash pages, each passing through about a dozen shared resources, from the plane and flash channel to the TSVs and ECC engine. Because slower memory changes batching, these accesses must be simulated in a closed loop rather than replayed. As shown in Figure 2, layers in HBFSim communicate through narrow interfaces. The frontend describes work in terms of model objects such as weight tensors and KV blocks. Policies map objects to devices and emit transaction graphs with explicit dependencies. The engine contains no LLM-specific logic. This separation lets users change one layer, for example, add a caching policy or an FTL, without touching the others. 3.1 Serving Frontend HBFSim accepts workloads at two granularities. In an address-level trace, a record is one memory access with optional data class, ar- rival time, and layer annotations; such traces are replayed directly. Detailed instruction-and-address tracing and cycle-level simulation incur substantial costs even for a small inference workload. For Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (bfloat16, batch size 1), a 32-token prefill followed by two fixed-token decode steps required 43.4 minutes for trace collection on an RTX 4000 Ada with NVBit [30]. The resulting 1,030-kernel traces occupy 98.3 GiB uncompressed, or 7.46 GiB in the compressed format consumed by Accel-Sim2.0 [20]. Full trace- driven simulation already takes 19.9 wall-clock hours even for a small model. For larger models, both the trace size and simulation time would become prohibitively large, rendering this approach unrealistic. In a request-level trace, a record is one inference request: its arrival time, prompt and output lengths, and prefix hashes [22, 31]. It contains no detailed memory accesses. Which bytes an inference step touches does not depend on the values it computes, only on the model architecture and on which requests the scheduler runs with how many tokens (for MoE models, also on the routed experts, which depend on the values and are therefore an input, recorded or synthetic). The frontend, ServeLoop, therefore regenerates the accesses of every step. Its scheduler replays the trace with vLLM’s continuous batching and chunked prefill [2, 11, 35], including paged KV, prefix sharing, and preemption. A compiler turns each iteration into the byte ranges that every operator reads or writes in weight tensors, KV blocks, and embedding rows, leaving addresses and memories to the policies. A decoding step of Llama-3.1-70B under the workload with 32 sequences and 6K tokens of context becomes 1.8 × 10 5 such transactions. The generated accesses are verified at three levels. Batching: given the same service times, the scheduler forms the same batches RACS ’26, November 17–20, 2026, Fukuoka, Japan as vLLM (Section 3.5). Addresses: the byte ranges and their order match 6,568 held-out warp streams captured with NVBit on an A100; the H200 we model has no capture, so its KV is read block by block, which changes the time per output token (TPOT) by at most 0.55% against the A100 order. Volume: the frontend counts each byte once, whereas prefill kernels refetch the same KV for other query heads or tiles, which GPU caches partly absorb, so prefill traffic is a lower bound. HBFSim times every batch, prefill and decode alike, using an operator-level GPU model. It decomposes each batch into opera- tors and computes each operator’s time from three components: a fixed overhead, a compute time, and a memory-access time. The compute time is derived from the operator’s FLOPs and a compute- throughput coefficient fitted to measured kernels. We obtain the memory-access time from HBFSim’s detailed simulation of HBM and HBF accesses, rather than an ideal-bandwidth assumption. To stay anchored to real GPU behavior, we fit each operator’s fixed overhead, compute throughput, and memory bandwidth from mea- sured kernels to establish a baseline time. During simulation, we replace the baseline’s ideal memory time with the simulated access time, while retaining the measured kernel’s additional memory overhead beyond the GPU’s peak bandwidth. The batch time is then the sum of all operator times. This design ensures that HBF latency and bandwidth directly affect each operator’s memory time, and thus the batch time, while the compute portion stays tied to measured GPU performance. 3.2 Memory Policies HBFSim provides two ways to organize HBM and HBF. In peer mode, HBM and HBF form one address space, and each object is stored in one of them. HBM is filled in a priority order and the rest overflows to HBF: weights first places the weights, then KV blocks in address order, retained prefixes included; KV first places the running sequences’ KV, then the weights, then the retained prefixes. In tiered mode, HBM caches objects stored in the HBF or other capacity tier in 4 MiB lines with LRU, FIFO, or decayed-LFU [23] replacement; decayed LFU evicts the line with the fewest recent accesses and halves all access counts periodically, as in frequency- based replacement [23]. Dirty data is tracked at 4 KiB granularity, and dirty KV is written back either eagerly, while compute leaves the link idle [12], or only when its line is evicted. KV released before eviction is discarded without being written. 3.3 Device Engine HBM. An HBM stack follows the JEDEC organization of its gen- eration, set by the number of channels and pseudo-channels and the pin rate. The following study uses HBM4 for analysis [8], with 32 channels of two pseudo-channels at 8 Gb/s per pin, or 2 TB/s per stack. Because our studies concern capacity tiers, HBFSim mod- els HBM at the pseudo-channel level rather than at the command level of DRAM simulators such as Ramulator 2.0 [16]. Requests are split into pseudo-channel transfers, groups of four pseudo-channels share an arbitration queue and a service timeline, and an average ac- cess latency and a bandwidth efficiency account for row activation and refresh. Li et al. HBF. As in the OCP specification, the model separates the device from its host-side management. The device has independent trans- mit and receive timelines for each channel, ordered page sensing within each bank, page buffers, ECC, and TSV transfers. It programs the pages of a block in order and, as the specification requires, erases a block when its first page is written. The organization of flash into channels, dies, planes, and blocks and the timing of reads, programs, and erases follow MQSim [29]. We reimplemented them because MQSim’s FTL runs inside an SSD, whereas HBF’s runs on the host, and HBF operations must share one timeline with HBM and the serving frontend. Like an SSD, and beyond the specification, each stack has a device-managed DRAM that buffers writes until a page is full and caches recently read pages. The host runs the FTL. It maps logical pages to physical ones and runs garbage collection, which picks victim blocks by their number of valid pages with a small weight for wear; static wear leveling is implemented but switched off in our studies. Since the specification forbids the device from moving valid data, garbage collection reads live pages into a copy buffer in HBM and writes them back. We implemented three mappings and keep each one’s index in HBM. Page-level mapping has an 8-byte entry per 4 KiB page; the whole table lives in flash as translation pages, and HBM caches part of it. Extent mapping keeps a sorted list of runs of consecutive pages, 48 B per run. Both write by appending and spread consecutive pages over all planes. Block- level mapping has one entry per 1 MiB logical block and keeps the block in one physical block on one plane, each page at a fixed offset. We model two consequences: NAND programs a block’s pages in order, so a page whose predecessors have not been written yet waits in the device DRAM; and any write that is not an in-order append copies the whole block to a fresh one. We do not stripe blocks over planes, because a copy would then move a 1.5 GiB stripe. Every mapping gets 0.1% of the HBF capacity in HBM, 3.1 GiB of the 96 GiB of two HBM4 stacks, and its lookups compete with the application’s traffic: with page-level mapping, one Llama-3.1-70B decoding step at 2 HBM + 6 HBF issues 1.0–1.7×10 7 lookups, one per flash page read. Other tiers. Host DRAM, CXL SSDs, and NVMe SSDs share one model consisting of a link, a controller, and media queues. A CXL SSD adds a device-side DRAM cache with FIFO replacement. 3.4 Simulation Speed To make full-iteration simulation tractable, we combine coarse- grained HBM approximation with exact HBF acceleration. Only HBM is approximated: scheduling transfers per 4 KiB chunk and pseudo-channel rather than per 32-byte burst runs an all-HBM for- ward pass 24.8× faster (134.7× for sequential reads), while keeping batch completion times within 0.04%. For HBF, the bottleneck is reserving roughly a dozen shared resources per page, as in SimpleSSD [9]; here we reduce per- reservation overhead without sacrificing accuracy. A first-fit calen- dar organizes each resource’s idle intervals into 64-interval leaves labeled with their maximum duration, so searches immediately bypass leaves with insufficient space. Multi-page reads are batched into groups of one page per plane to share stage-time calculations, reuse calendar lookup states across groups, and compute stride addresses from the first page, while the FTL updates free space only for planes whose state changes. The scheduler is checked against vLLM 0.26’s: both receive the same requests and the same measured batch times, and over 282 batches in ten test cases with staggered arrivals, shared prefixes, prefix eviction, and preemption, they form the same batches with the same token ranges, prefix hits, and completion times. The operator model is fitted to kernel measurements: on an A100 and an H200 NVL we timed the Marlin GEMMs and FlashAttention-2 paged attention that vLLM uses with 8-bit weights, inside whole layers under CUDA graphs, over 525 shapes per GPU spanning batch, query, and context sizes, and fitted each operator’s fixed overhead, compute rate, and memory rate by least squares. We then predict 64 whole-layer shapes that never entered the fit: the mean absolute error is 5.8% on the A100 and 5.0% on the H200, and the largest, 41.8% on the A100, occurs in Llama-3.1-70B layers whose batch mixes long and short contexts. Finally we run complete requests on each GPU, from the embedding to the output head, and compare each batch’s time: predicted and measured batch times differ by 10.2% on average on the A100 (Llama-3.1-8B, 46 batches) and by 5.8% on the H200 (Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.1-70B, 86 batches); for Llama-3.1-70B on the H200, the time to first token differs by 9.3–13.6% and TPOT by 4.6–7.0%. The host DRAM path is fitted to measured pinned-memory copies between an H200 NVL and its host (issue time, bandwidth per direction, fixed latency). HBM4 and HBF cannot be calibrated yet. Their interfaces follow the specifications; HBM’s access latency and bandwidth efficiency and HBF’s internal timing (4 𝜇s page read, 75 𝜇s program) and par- allelism are assumptions users can replace. Every default parameter records its source, published, from the literature, or assumed; 18 of the 30 parameter groups are assumptions. We model one accelerator package with eight memory stacks, each an HBM4 stack or an HBF stack (Table 1); we write 2 HBM + 6 HBF for a package of two HBM and six HBF stacks (2:6 in the figures, 2H6F in Table 3). We compare 1 HBM + 7 HBF, 2 HBM + 6 HBF, 4 HBM + 4 HBF, and 6 HBM + 2 HBF, whose HBM holds 43.4, 91.9, 188.9, and 285.9 GiB of data. The HBF stacks follow OCP speed grade 2, with 16 channels, one die per channel, 16 planes per die, and blocks of 256 pages of 4 KiB. Like an SSD, each HBF stack has a device DRAM of 0.1% of its flash that serves as write buffer and read cache. Unless noted otherwise, the host FTL uses page-level mapping and caches translation pages in 0.1% of the HBF capacity, reserved in HBM. We serve Llama-3.1-70B [5] with 8-bit weights (67.7 GiB) and a BF16 KV cache (320 KiB per token), and Qwen3-235B-A22B with FP8 weights (223.0 GiB for the 128 experts of each of its 94 MoE layers) and a BF16 KV cache (188 KiB per token); the figures label them 70B and 235B. Public traces carry no expert routes, so the 235B model routes every token to a uniformly random top-8 of its 128 experts, seeded by the token’s prefix; at 32 sequences a decode step reads 197.9 GiB of the 223 GiB of weights. GPU compute follows the H200 NVL operator profile (Section 3.5), which covers batches of up to 16; for larger batches we keep the per-FLOP and per-byte costs measured at 16. Workloads. A decode step reads the KV of every running se- quence, so what distinguishes workloads is how much context the sequences hold and how that context was produced. The public traces of Mooncake [22] and Qwen [31] are input-heavy (at most 29% of their requests have more than 62.5% of their tokens in the output), so no output-heavy workload can be drawn from them; their median request holds 5.5K–7.3K tokens. Prompts are private, so no KV is shared. We replay each workload through the scheduler with 32 sequences per batch and a prefix cache that retains 1M tokens (320 GiB of KV for Llama-3.1-70B, 188 GiB for Qwen3-235B-A22B). The first batch’s requests arrive spread over one request’s lifetime, so in the steady state the run- ning sequences are at every stage of their lifetimes. Among the steps in which every batch slot is busy while requests wait and the prefix cache is full, we take the one whose running sequences hold the median context and install its state as replayed, each KV block at its replayed address. We then measure a short window instead of a full replay: each sequence prefills a private 16-token suffix, which resumes it as a running request and yields its first token, and decodes seven more; TPOT is the mean time of these seven decode steps. The three workloads hold 5.2K, 6.3K, and 7.3K tokens of context on average, so a step reads 51–71 GiB of KV for Llama-3.1-70B and 30–42 GiB for Qwen3-235B-A22B, 40% more under long INPUT than under long OUTPUT, and writes one token of KV per sequence. 4.2 HBF Versus Other Capacity Tiers At 2 HBM + 6 HBF with weights first, the capacity tier serves 38– 65 GiB of running KV per step for Llama-3.1-70B and 145–157 GiB for Qwen3-235B-A22B, whose 223 GiB of weights exceed HBM: 115 GiB of weights and all 30–42 GiB of running KV. We keep this placement and replace the six HBF stacks with host DRAM, a CXL SSD, or an NVMe SSD of the same capacity (Figure 4a). HBF decodes 11.0–14.4× faster than host DRAM, 16.1–21.3× faster than the CXL SSD, and 86.6–115.0× faster than the NVMe SSD for Llama-3.1-70B, and 18.6–19.0×, 66.8–154.1×, and 150.3–154.1× faster for Qwen3- 235B-A22B. The step time is roughly the tier read divided by the tier’s bandwidth: six on-package HBF stacks serve 157 GiB in 0.17 s, PCIe-attached host DRAM in 3.2 s, and the NVMe SSD’s NAND at 6.6 GB/s in 26 s. The CXL SSD’s device DRAM (5% of its flash, 153.6 GiB) holds the spill of Llama-3.1-70B and of the first two Qwen3-235B-A22B workloads, so the CXL SSD stays within 1.5× of host DRAM there; the 157 GiB spill of long INPUT exceeds it and the CXL SSD is as slow as the NVMe SSD (26.0 s). We keep all 32 sequences in every system, so each tier serves the same spill; a real system would shrink the batch. An off-package tier occupies none of the package’s eight stack sites, which can then hold HBM. Figure 4b therefore compares seven systems on eight sites, all with KV first: 2 HBM + 6 HBF; 2 HBM with the HBF’s capacity off package as a CXL or NVMe SSD, alone or behind 256 GiB of host DRAM (one accelerator’s share of a 2 TiB server), leaving six sites empty; and 8 HBM with the CXL SSD, alone or behind host DRAM. With two HBM stacks, the weights that do not fit in HBM come from the tier in every step: 2 HBM + 6 HBF is 9.3–12.5× faster than 2 HBM + host DRAM + CXL SSD for Llama-3.1-70B and 19.1–19.5× for Qwen3-235B-A22B. Host DRAM holds the first 256 GiB of the tier, which covers both models’ weights, so the SSD behind it is never read and the NVMe and CXL variants coincide. The SSDs alone are 13.5–18.3× (CXL) and 70.8–98.0× (NVMe) slower than 2 HBM + 6 HBF for Llama-3.1- 70B, and 66.9–99.3× and 154.3–157.2× for Qwen3-235B-A22B. With eight HBM stacks (384 GiB), both working sets fit, no step reads the off-package tier, and TPOT is 49–55 ms: 1.4–1.5× below 2 HBM + 6 HBF for Llama-3.1-70B and 2.9× below it for Qwen3-235B-A22B. An off-package tier thus wins only when the sites it frees go to HBM and the step fits in that HBM; then a cheap tier serves as well as a fast one. Takeaway 1: HBF is most valuable under memory-capacity pressure. It offers little benefit when the working set fits in HBM, but substantially outperforms offloading to CPU memory, CXL SSDs, and NVMe SSDs once spilling occurs, for example when Qwen3-235B-A22B serves 32 sequences whose 253–265 GiB work- ing set exceeds the 188.9 GiB of HBM at 4 HBM + 4 HBF. Under a fixed stack budget, however, adding more HBM can hurt per- formance if the resulting loss of HBF bandwidth outweighs the reduction in spill traffic. 4.3 How Much HBM, and What Should It Hold? Capacity and placement. We vary the split between HBM and HBF (Figure 5). In peer mode, HBM should give priority to the running sequences’ KV. The working set of Llama-3.1-70B (119– 139 GiB) fits at 4 HBM + 4 HBF, where KV first and tiered mode reach the compute-bound 49–54 ms. At 2 HBM + 6 HBF, KV first takes 69–83 ms and weights first 75–95 ms, 4–14% more: it fills the HBM left after the weights with KV blocks in address order, retained prefixes included, and leaves 38–65 GiB of running KV in HBF per step, whereas KV first reads only weights from HBF (29–49 GiB). At 1 HBM + 7 HBF even KV first reads 8–28 GiB of running KV per step from HBF (89–98 ms). The working set of Qwen3-235B-A22B (253–265 GiB) exceeds HBM at all three splits. Its decode step is dominated by the 198 GiB of expert weights it reads, so KV first falls only gradually, from 163–170 ms at 1 HBM + 7 HBF and 152–160 ms at 2 HBM + 6 HBF to 115–128 ms at 4 HBM + 4 HBF, and weights first is 4–7% behind. At 1 HBM + 7 HBF the step takes only 7% longer than at 2 HBM + 6 HBF: seven HBF stacks serve the experts. The three workloads differ little: their contexts differ by 1K tokens, and TPOT follows (69, 76, and 83 ms with KV first at 2 HBM + 6 HBF): a step’s cost depends on how much context it reads, not on how it was produced. Tiered mode. Tiered mode matches peer mode with KV first when the working set fits in HBM and, with LRU or FIFO, is 1.7– 2.2× slower for Llama-3.1-70B and 1.3–2.4× for Qwen3-235B-A22B when it does not. Each step reads the working set in the same order, a cyclic pattern larger than HBM, so LRU evicts almost every 4 MiB line before it is reused and the step rereads the whole working set from HBF, 117–137 GiB for Llama-3.1-70B and 231–243 GiB for Qwen3-235B-A22B, instead of only the spill. This is why 4 HBM + 4 HBF is slower than 2 HBM + 6 HBF for Qwen3-235B-A22B in tiered mode (275–291 against 201–211 ms): four HBF stacks serve the same reread instead of six. At 1 HBM + 7 HBF the single HBM stack, which also absorbs every refill as a write, becomes the limit at 1.4–1.6 TB/s of its 2.0. Replacement. No policy wins everywhere. FIFO rereads the same bytes as LRU in another order: within 1% of LRU for Qwen3- 235B-A22B and 1–20% faster for Llama-3.1-70B. Decayed LFU keeps the lines read most often: for Llama-3.1-70B at 2 HBM + 6 HBF it keeps the running KV in HBM and refills the weights every step, the division of KV first, and takes 84–90 ms, 37–48% less than LRU. At 1 HBM + 7 HBF, where the running KV (51–71 GiB) no longer fits, the same policy is the slowest, 261–308 ms, 1.4× LRU: it evicts its newest lines first. For Qwen3-235B-A22B it cuts LRU’s time by 7–10% at 1 HBM + 7 HBF and 22–31% at the next two splits but stays 1.0–1.8× above KV first: a newly filled line starts with a count of one, so the expert weights, which every step reads once, keep being evicted and refilled. 240 4:4 HBM:HBF 150 160 100 80 50 0 Zipf 1 64% Zipf 1.5 46% Zipf 2 34% 0 Zipf 1 64% Zipf 1.5 46% Zipf 2 34% Expert popularity (share of experts a step reads) Figure 6: Qwen3-235B-A22B under skewed expert popularity (balanced workload; legend as in Figure 5): a token’s top-8 experts are drawn with weight (𝑟 + 1) −𝛼 over a seeded per- layer rank 𝑟 . Tick labels: share of the experts a step reads. Hot experts. The uniform router is the worst case for a cache. We therefore rerun Qwen3-235B-A22B with a Zipf router of ex- ponent 𝛼 (Figure 6), so that a step reads 64%, 46%, and 34% of the experts at 𝛼 = 1, 1.5, and 2 instead of 88%. At 4 HBM + 4 HBF, where 𝛼 = 1.5 leaves 135–147 GiB in 188.9, decayed LFU takes 0.83–0.87 of the KV-first time and LRU 0.89–1.00; at 𝛼 = 2 they take 0.78 and 0.81–0.83: the cache keeps every layer’s hot experts, whereas the address-ordered split keeps whole early layers and misses those of the late ones. At 2 HBM + 6 HBF the split still wins at every exponent: decayed LFU stays 1.07–1.10× above KV first, because the 26 whole layers in HBM save their cold experts too while the cache spends its remainder on cold lines that rarely recur, and LRU and FIFO 1.4–1.5× above. When each mode wins. One quantity separates the two modes in Figures 5 and 6: the set a step reads against the HBM capacity. Peer mode with KV first wins whenever that set exceeds HBM, and the margin must be real: at 𝛼 = 1 and 4 HBM + 4 HBF the 180 GiB set, 144 GiB of weights and 36 of KV, nominally fits in 188.9, yet FIFO rereads 193 GiB per step, the set in 4 MiB lines, and LRU 161. Tiered mode wins only when the set fits with room to spare and its reuse is spread across layers, which an address-ordered split cannot follow; where the set fits outright, the two modes are equal. Takeaway 2: Under the evaluated workloads and 4 MiB cache-line configuration, the tested replacement policies in- cur substantial refill traffic when the active working set ex- ceeds HBM capacity. None of the evaluated policies matches peer RACS ’26, November 17–20, 2026, Fukuoka, Japan Long OUTPUT Balanced Long INPUT 100 Throughput (k tokens/s) Page-level Decode Index (MiB) 1000 6:2 0.4 10 0.2 1 400 200 0 0.0 8 16 32 64 8 16 32 64 8 16 32 Extent Request time (s) HBM:HBF stacks 2:6 4:4 TPOT (ms) 1:7 Li et al. 64 Long Balanced Long OUTPUT INPUT Block Prefill 150 100 50 0 Long Balanced Long OUTPUT INPUT Batch size Figure 7: Decode throughput of Qwen3-235B-A22B against the batch size, peer mode with KV first. mode with KV first once the set a step reads exceeds HBM, and they beat it only when that set fits with room to spare, because none captures the distinct access patterns, mutability, and lifetimes of inference data. Effective HBF management therefore requires inference-aware placement and migration rather than generic cache replacement. Batch size. We repeat the Qwen3-235B-A22B study in peer mode with KV first at batches of 8, 16, 32, and 64, each from its own replay (Figure 7). Throughput grows 2.1–3.0× from batch 8 to 64 at 6 HBM + 2 HBF and 2.9–3.5× at 2 HBM + 6 HBF and 1 HBM + 7 HBF, while TPOT grows from 37 ms to 67–117 ms and from 74–84 ms to 186–205 ms. The working set grows with the batch, to 283, 295, and 306 GiB at batch 64; only long OUTPUT still fits in the 285.9 GiB of 6 HBM + 2 HBF, its 520 tokens/s compare with 420 and 353 for the other two, and tiered mode with LRU, 67 ms where the working set fits, takes 503 and 672 ms once it exceeds HBM by 3% and 7%. With one to four HBM stacks the expert weights come from HBF in any case; the second pair of HBM stacks is worth 38% of throughput at batch 8 but 9% at batch 64. Write path. A decode step writes too little KV to compare ways of writing it, so we also serve 112, 56, and 38 requests of the three workloads from an empty KV state at 2 HBM + 6 HBF (outputs capped at 8 tokens), which writes 46–47 GiB of KV per workload. Writing the KV that does not fit in HBM straight to HBF, writing all KV into HBM and to HBF when its line is evicted, and draining it to HBF in the background give the same mean request time within 1.5%, because prefill is compute-bound and each HBF stack buffers writes in its device DRAM. The background drain, however, writes 70–71 GiB to flash, 1.2–1.6× as much as write-back on eviction (45– 60 GiB). In decode, KV first never programs an HBF page, while tiered mode with LRU programs 61,000–65,000 pages per step for Qwen3-235B-A22B as it evicts dirty KV. Takeaway 3: KV data should be prioritized in HBM and moved to HBF only under capacity pressure. KV is continu- ously appended during decoding, making its placement a primary determinant of HBF write traffic. Allocating KV to HBF only when it must leave HBM incurs no performance loss in our experiments, whereas proactive migration creates avoidable writes for KV entries that may be freed shortly. 4.4 Flash Translation and Endurance In decode, HBF mostly serves reads, so we ask what the FTL costs on the read path and how fast writes wear HBF. We compare the three mappings of Sec- tion 3.3 at 2 HBM + 6 HBF with weights first, so that the running KV is read from HBF (Figure 8). A decode step writes almost nothing, so we also run the prefill windows of Section 4.3 (46–47 GiB of new KV each). All three receive the same 3.1 GiB of HBM, but only page-level mapping uses a sizable part of it: 97–152 MiB of transla- tion pages for the pages a decode step touches, against 0.9 MiB for the extent index and 10 MiB for the block index. Extent mapping stays within 0.5% of page-level mapping in decode and in prefill: KV is written and read in long runs, so one index entry serves many pages. Block-level mapping is 4.2–4.3× slower in decode (324–399 against 75–95 ms), because a block lies on one plane, which reads its 256 pages one after another in about 1.0 ms, whereas the other two mappings spread the same pages over all planes; prefill, which spends more of its time in compute, hides part of this and is 1.5× slower. Takeaway 4: HBF mapping should preserve internal par- allelism rather than maximize address granularity. Decode reads weights and KV in long sequential runs, so one translation serves many pages. An extent mapping that stripes each run across all planes matches a page-level table at a fraction of its memory, whereas a block-level mapping that keeps each block on a single plane serializes its page reads and slows decoding considerably. HBFSim measures the share of this KV that reaches HBF with weights first (87.5–100%) and replays each workload’s KV writes and releases (about 1 TiB, twice the stack’s capacity) through one HBF stack with garbage collection, which gives the flash bytes erased per written byte in steady state, the quantity that consumes P/E cycles. With either mapping this is 1.0 within 0.1%: KV is appended and freed in bulk, so one block with no valid page left is erased per MiB written. Block-level mapping programs 1.5–3.5% fewer pages, because pages that wait in the device DRAM for their block’s unwritten prefix are dropped when a sequence ends, but their block is still erased. Assuming 100,000 P/E cycles, as for the SLC NAND used in HBF designs [32], Table 3 gives the resulting lifetime: 24–83 months for Llama-3.1-70B and 40–141 months for Qwen3-235B-A22B, in proportion to the HBF stacks that share the writes and the same with either mapping: how long HBF lasts is set by how much KV reaches flash. Takeaway 5: HBF endurance is a first-order system con- straint. Under baseline inference workloads, KV spill generates enough writes to make projected HBF lifetime a major challenge even when performance is acceptable. Practical HBF systems there- fore require write reduction and endurance-aware management. 4.5 Which HBF Parameters Matter? The HBF specification is still a draft, so we ask which device pa- rameters the results depend on, taking Llama-3.1-70B on the three workloads at 2 HBM + 6 HBF with KV first, where a step reads 29–49 GiB of weights from HBF (69–83 ms per token), and changing one parameter at a time (Figure 9). Only the rate at which the flash array senses pages matters. Doubling the page read time to 8 𝜇s raises TPOT by 30–42%, 16 𝜇s by 91–126%, and the 40 𝜇s of conventional NAND by 3.7–4.8×; halving the planes per die at equal capacity has the same effect as doubling the read time (29–40% for 8 planes, 87–121% for 4). The interface does not matter: speed grade 3 doubles grade 2’s 1.5 TB/s and changes TPOT by 0.1%, and grades 1 and 2 on 8 channels are equally 29–40% slower, only because their stacks have half the planes. A plane senses one 4 KiB page per read time, so a stack’s 256 planes deliver 0.26 TB/s at 4 𝜇s, a sixth of the interface. The write side is invisible in decode, even without the device DRAM: with KV first a step appends its KV in HBM and programs no HBF DISCUSSION Limitations. Our case studies reproduce one decoding step per workload, seven tokens per running sequence, and one prefill win- dow per workload for the write path and the mapping comparison, without garbage collection, so TPOT omits its interference with reads. We model one accelerator; tensor or pipeline parallelism would give each a share of the weights and KV. The studies com- bine an H200 compute profile, extended beyond its measured batch of 16, with HBM4 and HBF, a pairing that does not exist today, so HBF timing and endurance remain assumptions. The lifetime estimates apply a published serving load around the clock to the HBF write share and write amplification that HBFSim measures, and assume perfect wear leveling. Extending HBFSim. New memory policies use the policy in- terface, new FTL schemes the host mapping interface, new HBF generations the device configuration, and new models, traces, and GPUs their descriptors, importers, or operator profiles. 6 RELATED WORK HBF and hybrid HBM–flash memory. H3 [7] and SK hynix [27] evaluate hybrid HBM+HBF organizations with projected device parameters. FlashAccel co-designs data layout and storage man- agement for HBF [32]. Petrucci et al. compare HBF with LPDDR analytically and identify writes as the limit for offloading KV to flash [21]. HBFSim lets such designs be compared on the same workloads; our endurance results quantify the write problem they point out. Memory and storage simulators. Ramulator 2.0 [16] and DRAMsim3 [14] model DRAM at the command level. MQSim [29] and FEMU [13] model SSDs behind an NVMe interface, with map- ping, GC, and wear leveling inside the device, and Cylon [34] emu- lates CXL SSDs with a DRAM cache in the device. HBFSim follows MQSim’s approach to the flash organization and Cylon’s device class for the CXL SSD, but treats HBF as memory with a host-side FTL whose metadata competes with the application in HBM. LLM serving simulators. Vidur [1], LLMServingSim [3], Fron- tier [6], and ASTRA-sim [33] simulate scheduling, computation, and communication for LLM inference, LLMCompass [36] adds operator-level modeling with mapping search, and GTSim [4] and Accel-Sim [10, 20] model GPU microarchitecture. They represent memory by its capacity and bandwidth; HBFSim models the de- vices at the transaction level, flash management included, under a validated scheduler. 7 CONCLUSION HBF could give accelerators an order of magnitude more memory, but only if systems use it in ways that suit flash. HBFSim lets researchers test these choices before hardware exists. Our case studies support five takeaways. HBF is most valuable under capacity pressure, where it keeps TPOT 11.0–19.0× lower than host DRAM and 86.6–154.1× lower than an NVMe SSD. Conventional cache replacement is a poor fit for HBM–HBF tiering: no policy matches RACS ’26, November 17–20, 2026, Fukuoka, Japan peer mode with KV first once the set a step reads exceeds HBM, and a cache wins only when that set fits with room to spare. HBM should hold the running sequences’ KV and HBF the read-only weights; KV should move to HBF only when it must leave HBM. The mapping should preserve the flash array’s parallelism, which an extent index does at a fraction of a page table’s memory. Endurance is a first-order constraint: at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. We release HBFSim so that others can replace our assumptions with measurements. REFERENCES [1] Amey Agrawal, Nitin Kedia, Jayashree Mohan, Ashish Panwar, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S.
